reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Distinguish irritant contact dermatitis (direct chemical or physical damage, no prior sensitisation, often stinging or burning) from allergic contact dermatitis (a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is typically itchy)
The distribution of the rash is the key clue to the culprit; sharply demarcated eruptions localised to sites of contact point to an external cause
Common irritants include water, soaps, detergents, and solvents, while frequent allergens include nickel, fragrances, preservatives, rubber accelerators, and topical medicaments
Acute lesions are erythematous, oedematous, and vesicular; chronic exposure produces dryness, scaling, fissuring, and lichenification
Patch testing is the definitive method to identify a contact allergen, whereas irritant dermatitis is largely a clinical diagnosis
Cornerstone management is identification and avoidance of the offending agent alongside barrier restoration with emollients and, for flares, topical corticosteroids
Occupational exposure is a common driver (e.g. hairdressers, healthcare and construction workers), so take a detailed work and hobby history
reference.pathophysiology: Contact dermatitis has two principal mechanisms. Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct, non-immunological damage to the epidermal barrier by chemical or physical agents, triggering innate inflammation; severity relates to the concentration and duration of exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction: after an initial sensitisation phase in which small-molecule haptens bind skin proteins and prime allergen-specific T cells, re-exposure elicits an inflammatory eczematous response over one to several days. Repeated insult impairs the barrier further, perpetuating inflammation and, over time, chronic lichenified changes.
additionalDifferentials: Psoriasis on the hands or feet
Cellulitis when acute unilateral limb involvement mimics infection
additionalInvestigations: Patch testing to identify causative allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis
Detailed occupational, cosmetic, and hobby exposure history
Skin swabs if secondary bacterial infection is suspected
Skin scrapings or mycology to exclude dermatophyte infection
Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Widespread or erythrodermic involvement with systemic upset
Rapidly spreading eruption with fever suggesting secondary infection or an alternative diagnosis
Airborne or facial involvement with eyelid swelling affecting vision
Occupational disease threatening ability to work and requiring formal assessment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent when the causative agent is identified and avoided; persistent exposure, especially occupational, leads to chronic relapsing dermatitis and may necessitate a change of work.
pitfalls: Failing to perform patch testing and thus missing a treatable allergen
Overlooking a relevant occupational or cosmetic exposure in the history
Assuming persistent hand eczema is purely irritant when a superimposed allergy exists
Applying a topical product that itself contains a sensitising allergen and perpetuates the dermatitis
management: Identify and avoid the offending irritant or allergen as the cornerstone of management, guided by patch testing for suspected allergic contact dermatitis
Restore the skin barrier with regular emollients and protective measures such as gloves and appropriate personal protective equipment
Treat flares with topical corticosteroids, using topical calcineurin inhibitors for sensitive sites
Treat secondary bacterial infection with antibiotics where present
Consider phototherapy or systemic immunosuppression for severe, chronic or refractory disease
Advise on occupational modification, since persistent exposure leads to chronic relapsing disease and may necessitate a change of work
